Author: @SponsorChecker
Content:
Sponsor Checker

 ↓

Proton Mail is actually a pretty good service for privacy, it's end to end encrypted, which basically means that no one, even Proton Mail will be able to see your emails, that is except for you. It has plenty of features that set it apart from other services, and if you want to get away from Google's grasp and have more privacy when it comes to what you do online then Proton may be for you.

Here are my pros and cons laid out.

Pros:

End to end encryption
Easy to use
Feature rich
Plenty of ways to customize your experience.

Cons:

While it's not much, Proton Mail is a paid service, which is definitely a down side when most email services are free.

Overall I can recommend Proton Mail if you're willing to pay a bit extra for privacy, you can use Linus' link in the description to get your first month free and support the channel.

Author: @Brazbit
Content:
The door blocking the electrical panel is such a bad idea. It will be so tempting to put something in the way of the path of the door resulting in not being able to get to it when needed. Plus obscuring the panel could result in disaster if no one can find the panel in an emergency. It would be an electrical code violation in the US, not sure about Canada.

We recently had a situation where an older building where it took four of us over an hour to locate the electrical panel in an emergency because it was in a closet behind hanging clothes. Had the problem been slightly worse that delay could have caused serious damage. 

The panel not having its own door/dead front like that is also concerning, but there are panels specially designed to not require one. Hopefully this is one of them, which it may be since there doesn't appear to be hinges or a latch for one.

Author: @Kinkajou1015
Content:
My only complaints relate to the Federation ship. It is an Ambassador class, so the only Enterprise it could be is NCC-1701-C which doesn't fit since the Enterprise-C never encountered the Borg and was destroyed by Romulans while attempting to provide aid to Klingons (Battle of Narendra III, see The Next Generation: Yesterday's Enterprise, S03E15). It's also missing the registration markings, so it could be NCC-26517 the USS Excalibur, the USS Horatio (supposedly NCC-10532), the USS Yamaguchi (NCC-26510), or the USS Zhukov (NCC-62136). 

My headcannon is it's not The Enterprise but actually The Yamaguchi and it's an artists recreation of a moment during the Battle of Wolf 359, where the lone surviving Federation vessel makes a bold move to escape the Borg tractor beams and jump to warp.

Having said all of that, I was hoping it would have been a Voyager model instead. David's Quadrant, Delta Quadrant, eh, ehhh?

Author: @NightHawkATL
Content: Most home audio speakers are 8 Ohms and most car speakers are 4 Ohms. Some bi-amp speakers for home audio will be 8 Ohms and connecting the 2 pairs of terminals together in parallel will keep them at 8 Ohms. When using speakers that are "bi-amp" with 4 total terminals, it is better to use 2 pairs of speaker cables and not combining them for the best sound but that also means that you need a receiver that supports them. If you have a cheaper receiver that doesn't support them and you parallel the terminals together, just make sure the receiver's amp isn't over the wattage rating of the speakers RMS total wattage to protect the speakers from getting blown.

Author: @Imjeezus
Content:
Rule of thumb is to always set resistance too high than too low. Most home theater speakers are 6ohm and up anyways. Worst case if the resistance is too high (6ohm and up) is you're just under powering the speakers. But if resistance is too low (4ohm or less) and you have say 8ohm speakers, well you are now effectively doubling the power through them at all volumes. This could easily blow the speaker or your amp or both. 

You can always take two 8ohm speakers and wire in parallel to get to a 4ohm resistance if changing the resistance on your amp isn't an option.

Author: @K-Anator
Content:
My parents bought a $300 sound bar, I forget the brand, but it's absolute garbage compared to my cobbled together system. 
I use an AKAI AM-A302 from 1986 that I got out of someone's shop when they were cleaning it out, and a pair of Kenwood LSK-2000 speakers I picked up for CA$15 at Value Village, plus a standalone Yamaha sub that was free. 
I've also got a second down firing sub, it's made from a rehoused 12" woofer that was with the AKAI system, it was the only salvageable speaker; a humid shop does terrible things to the foams of high end speakers over the course of 30 years, and I couldn't find adequate replacement cones to make them worth saving.

My audio doesn't get muddy at high volume though, and you can really feel the bass. Two things my parent's sound bar fails at. 
I would pick my $15 2.2 system over the $300 sound bar any day.

You worry too much about impedance. If the amplifier has the balls to deal with the dips, you're all good.

Author: @AV-Obsessed
Content: Another top from an AV expert. Never set the impedance switch on an AV receiver to anything other than 8 Ohms. I know it sounds crazy but that switch doesn't do what poeple think. All the Impedance switch does is cut current to the amplifier portion of the AVR reducing the amount of power it can output to the speakers. They do this because AVRs  need to hit certain efficiency numbers so when they are being tested by companies like UL Labs they run them with the impedance set lower for lower impedance loads and the receiver will not draw more power during those tests but when a home user sets it to the lower setting all you are doing is cutting you available power by as much a 50%!

Here’s a great tech tip. Always use the highest impedance mode (smallest number) on your receiver. Those switches are simply there for things like energy star ratings. So, if there was a 6ohm or 4ohm setting, always use that, even if you have 8ohm speakers.

Slightly longer version: the receiver will run hotter if you do this, so make sure it’s well ventilated (duh), and your speakers will be less likely to kill themselves due to receiving clipped power signals.

Author: @michaelfrei9296
Content:
The floating pc should be hanging rather than supported from below. Use the same wall bracket (mounted one pc height higher), turn the pc upside down, and mount from above rather than below. You can even bend some flat bars with a gentle curve attached at the ends to the pc and at the lowest point in the curve to the wall mount. That way the bar will operate as a spring to keep the thing from sagging, like if the bars were flat.

Also, probably too late, but you could have fed the wire for the enterprise through the center of a hollow aluminum rod.
